paragraphs: At our next camp it was ordered that every man in the army should collect carts, each one according to his circumstances. Seven hundred carts … were brought in. The order given to Ustad 'Ali-quli* was that these carts should be joined together in Ottoman fashion, but using ropes of raw hide instead of chains, and that between every two carts 5 or 6 mantelets should be fixed, behind which the matchlockmen were to stand to fire. …

People estimated the army opposing us at 100,000 men; Ibrahim's elephants and those of his amirs were said to be about 1000. In his hands was the treasure of two forbears. … Ibrahim could neither content his braves, nor share out his treasure. How should he content his braves when he was ruled by avarice and had a craving insatiable to pile coin on coin? …

… From that same position [in front of the centre] Ustad 'Ali-quli made good discharge of firingi shots; Mustafa the commissary for his part made excellent discharge of zarb-zan shots from the left hand of the centre. Our right, left, centre and turning-parties having surrounded the enemy, rained arrows down on him and fought ungrudgingly. … By God's mercy and kindness, this difficult affair was made easy for us! In one half-day, that armed mass was laid upon the earth.

paragraphs: Whereas the power of conferring Indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church; and she has, even in the most ancient times, used the said power, delivered unto her of God; the sacred holy Synod teaches, and enjoins, that the use of Indulgences, for the Christian people most salutary, and approved of by the authority of sacred Councils, is to be retained in the Church; and It condemns with anathema those who either assert, that they are useless; or who deny that there is in the Church the power of granting them.

In granting them, however, It desires that, in accordance with the ancient and approved custom in the Church, moderation be observed; lest, by excessive facility, ecclesiastical discipline be enervated. And being desirous that the abuses which have crept therein, and by occasion of which this honourable name of Indulgences is blasphemed by heretics, be amended and corrected. It ordains generally by this decree, that all evil gains for the obtaining thereof, … be wholly abolished.

paragraphs: Perhaps no more daring experiment has been tried on a large scale upon the face of the earth than that embodied in the Ottoman Ruling Institution. … The Ottoman system deliberately took slaves and made them ministers of state; it took boys from the sheep-run and the plow-tail and made them courtiers and the husbands of princesses; it took young men whose ancestors had borne the Christian name for centuries, and made them rulers in the greatest of Mohammedan states, and soldiers and generals in invincible armies whose chief joy was to beat down the Cross and elevate the Crescent. It never asked its novices, "Who was your father?" or "What do you know?" or even "Can you speak our tongue?"; but it studied their faces and their frames and said, "You shall be a soldier, and if you show yourself worthy, a general," or, "You shall be a scholar and a gentleman, and if the ability lies in you, a governor and a prime minister."

Grandly disregarding that fabric of fundamental customs which is called "human nature," and those religious and social prejudices which are thought to be almost as deep as life itself, the Ottoman system took children forever from parents, discouraged family cares among its members through their most active years, allowed them no certain hold on property, gave them no definite promise that their sons and daughters would profit by their success and sacrifice, raised and lowered them with no regard for ancestry or previous distinction, taught them a strange law, ethics, and religion, and ever kept them conscious of a sword raised above their heads which might put an end at any moment to a brilliant career along a matchless path of human glory.

paragraphs: … Shah Isma'il resolved that, with his assumption of the kingly rank, the Shi'a faith should become not merely the State religion but the only tolerated creed. This decision caused anxiety even to some of the Shi'a divines of Tabriz, who, on the night preceding Isma'il's coronation, represented to him that of the two or three hundred thousand inhabitants of that city at least two-thirds were Sunnis; that the Shi'a formula had not been publicly uttered from the pulpit since the time of the Imams themselves; and that if the majority of the people refused to accept a Shi'a ruler, it would be difficult to deal with the situation which would then arise. To this Shah Isma'il replied, "I am committed to this action; God and the Immaculate Imams are with me, and I fear no one; by God's help, if the people utter one word of protest, I will draw the sword and leave not one of them alive." Nor did he content himself with glorifying 'Ali and his descendants, but ordained the public cursing of the first three Caliphs of the Sunnis, Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman, and that all who heard the cursing should respond "May it be more, not less!" … or suffer death in case of refusal.

… [Isma'il's] foreign relations … were chiefly with three Powers, … the Timurids …; the formidable Uzbeks of Transoxiana; and the Ottoman Turks. With the last two, rigid Sunnis in both cases, the relations of Persia were, and continued to be, uniformly hostile. …

… [A letter] from Sultan Salim to Shah Isma'il, … dated … April, 1514 … , written in the most arrogant and offensive tone, calls on Isma'il to repent of his heresies and evil practices, especially the cursing of "the two Shaykhs" (Abu Bakr and 'Umar), and threatens, should he continue obdurate, to invade and wrest from him "the lands which he has usurped by violence."

X6.title: Estimated Yearly Income of the Ottoman Sultan from Kharaj (Tribute), Selected Regions, 1530s
X6.text: The estimate comes from a pamphlet by Junis Bey, chief interpreter at the Ottoman court, which also reports the views of Alvise Gritti, a Venetian merchant in Istanbul. Lybyer dated it to between 1530 and 1537, most likely 1533. He judged it the lowest estimate of the sultan's income and probably the most accurate for the regions it covers. Kharaj here means the tax or tribute each region sent to the sultan; Lybyer defines kharaj as a tax or tribute, in money or in goods, on lands held by non-Muslims. A ducat was a gold coin. Baghdad, taken by the Ottomans in 1534, is not listed. Only regions are shown; a smaller amount from other sources is left out. The table shows only income that reached the sultan, not all taxes collected in the empire.
X6.source: Albert Howe Lybyer, The Government of the Ottoman Empire in the Time of Suleiman the Magnificent (1913), p. 179 (Italian original printed in Appendix II, p. 273)

paragraphs: Djouder Pasha was the commander-in-chief of the Moorish army. He had at his disposal for the purposes of an expedition to the Soudan only a small force of something under 4000 men, but they were well armed with muskets—which were apparently unknown to the western armies of the Soudan—they were well mounted, well disciplined, well equipped with tents and medical stores, and, … sufficiently well provisioned. Their organisation had been reformed on the model of the Turks, with whom the armies of Morocco had had more than one occasion to measure their strength.

A little steel-coloured man with blue eyes, at the head of such a force, was in a position to play, if he chose, amid the rich and supine populations of the Soudan, a part not unlike that of the leader of a pack of wolves among flocks of sheep. …

… Morocco found its cause of quarrel with Songhay in the possession of the salt mines of Tegazza. … They furnished the principal salt supply of the Soudan, and their possession was therefore a matter of supreme importance to Songhay. …

… To the last moment the officials of Songhay refused to believe that the Moorish army would succeed in reaching the river. Finally, however, an army of 12,000 horse and 30,000 foot was put in motion. On the 12th of April, 1591*, the forces met at a place called Tenkoudibo, which I have not been able to identify, … The battle resulted in the absolute defeat of the Songhay army. The cavalry was routed, the chivalry of Songhay fled. …

paragraphs: … the King, as proprietor of the land, makes over a certain quantity to military men, as an equivalent for their pay; and this grant is called jah-ghir, or, as in Turkey, timar … Similar grants are made to governors, in lieu of their salary, and also for the support of their troops, on condition that they pay a certain sum annually to the King out of any surplus revenue that the land may yield. …

The persons thus put in possession of the land, whether as timariots, governors, or contractors, have an authority almost absolute over the peasantry, … and nothing can be imagined more cruel and oppressive than the manner in which it is exercised. There is no one before whom the injured peasant, artisan, or tradesman can pour out his just complaints; no great lords, parliaments, or judges of local courts, exist, as in France, to restrain the wickedness of those merciless oppressors …

… a question will naturally arise, whether it would not be more advantageous for the King as well as for the people, if the former ceased to be sole possessor of the land, and the right of private property were recognised in the Indies as it is with us? I have carefully compared the condition of European states, where that right is acknowledged, with the condition of those countries where it is not known, and am persuaded that the absence of it among the people is injurious to the best interests of the Sovereign himself.

… The peasant cannot avoid asking himself this question: 'Why should I toil for a tyrant who may come to-morrow and lay his rapacious hands upon all I possess and value …?'—The Timariots, Governors, and Revenue contractors, on their part reason in this manner: '… We may be deprived of it in a single moment, and our exertions would benefit neither ourselves nor our children. Let us draw from the soil all the money we can, though the peasant should starve or abscond …'

paragraphs: … The territories, which bear the name of Persia, and are ruled by the Sophi, or Kizilbash as the Turks call him, are less fertile than our country, and even such crops as they bear are laid waste by the inhabitants in time of invasion in hopes of starving out the enemy, so that it is very dangerous for an army to invade Persia, if it be not furnished with abundant supplies. …

From this you will see that it is the patience, self-denial, and thrift of the Turkish soldier that enable him to face the most trying circumstances, and come safely out of the dangers that surround him. What a contrast to our men! … It makes me shudder to think of what the result of a struggle between such different systems must be; one of us must prevail and the other be destroyed, at any rate we cannot both exist in safety. On their side is the vast wealth of their empire, unimpaired resources, experience and practice in arms, a veteran soldiery, an uninterrupted series of victories, readiness to endure hardships, union, order, discipline, thrift, and watchfulness. On ours are found an empty exchequer, luxurious habits, exhausted resources, broken spirits, a raw and insubordinate soldiery, and greedy generals … The only obstacle is Persia, whose position on his [the sultan's] rear forces the invader to take precautions. The fear of Persia gives us a respite, but it is only for a time. …

I will now give you another conversation with Roostem*, that you may understand how widely the Persians are separated from the Turks by religion. He once asked me if war was still going on between the Kings of Spain and France. On my replying that it was, 'What right have they,' said he, 'to wage war on each other, when they are united by the ties of religion?' 'The same,' said I, 'as you have to fight with the Persians. There are cities, provinces, and kingdoms about which they are at variance.' 'It is quite a different case,' said Roostem, 'for we, you must know, hate the Persians worse, and consider them more impious than we do you Christians.'

paragraphs: … The force at the disposal of the Shah originally consisted of some sixty thousand Kizilbash horsemen, who would obey none but their chiefs. Consequently he was unable to give a command to any one outside the Kizilbash themselves, in whose hands the entire power lay. To meet this difficulty he halved the numbers of the tribal contingents and organized a body of ten thousand cavalry and twelve thousand infantry, paid and officered by the crown.

Allah Verdi Beg, the celebrated Commander-in-Chief, was quick to see the advantages of the Sherley mission*, which included among its members a cannon-founder. With his assistance and thanks to the Sherleys, batteries of artillery were formed, as well as regiments of regular infantry. Indeed, mainly through the initiative of our fellow-countrymen, a revolution was effected in the military organization, and in place of a feudal force of horsemen Persia soon possessed an army fit to meet that of Turkey in the field. …

paragraphs: On the southeast side, they have got the kingdoms of Kazan and Astrakhan. These were won from the Tartar by the late emperor Ivan Vasilowich, father to the emperor that now is … Northward out of the country of Siberia he hath laid unto his realm a great breadth and length of ground, from Wichida to the river of Obba, about a 1000 miles space: so that he is bold to write himself now, the great commander of Siberia. …

As for the countries of Pechora and Permia, and that part of Siberia which he hath now under him, they are kept by as easy means as they were first got, viz., rather by showing than by using of arms. First, he hath stored the country with as many Russes as there are natives, and hath there some few soldiers in garrison, enough to keep them under. Secondly, his officers and magistrates there are of his own Russe people, and he changeth them very often … Thirdly, he divideth them into many small governments, like a staff broke in many small pieces: so that they have no strength, being severed … Fourthly, he provided that the people of the country have neither armour nor money, being taxed and pilled so often as he thinketh good …

In Siberia (where he goeth on in pursuing his conquest) he hath divers castles and garrisons, to the number of six thousand soldiers of Russes and Polonians, and sendeth many new supplies thither, to plant and to inhabit as he winneth ground.

paragraphs: The Tsar labored at the reform of fashions, or, more properly speaking, of dress. Until that time the Russians had always worn long beards, which they cherished and preserved with much care, allowing them to hang down on their bosoms, without even cutting the moustache. … The Tsar, in order to reform that custom, ordered that gentlemen, merchants, and other subjects, except priests and peasants, should each pay a tax … if they wished to keep their beards … Officials were stationed at the gates of the towns to collect that tax, which the Russians regarded as an enormous sin on the part of the Tsar and as a thing which tended to the abolition of their religion.

These insinuations, which came from the priests, occasioned the publication of many pamphlets in Moscow, where for that reason alone the Tsar was regarded as a tyrant and a pagan; and there were many old Russians who, after having their beards shaved off, saved them preciously, in order to have them placed in their coffins, fearing that they would not be allowed to enter heaven without their beards. As for the young men, they followed the new custom with the more readiness, as it made them appear more agreeable to the fair sex.

From the reform in beards we may pass to that of clothes. Their garments, like those of the Orientals, were very long, reaching to the heel. The Tsar issued an ordinance abolishing that costume, commanding all the boyars (nobles) and all those who had positions at the court to dress after the French fashion …

paragraphs: This incomparable mosque was built by Sultan Suleiman on one-half of the unoccupied half of the summit of the lofty hill on which had been erected, by Mohammed II, the old Serai. Suleiman having assembled all the thousands of perfect masters in architecture, building, stone-hewing, and marble-cutting, who were found in the dominions of the house of 'Osman, three whole years were employed in laying the foundations. …

… This vast structure of azure stone is more circular than the cupola of Aya Sofiyah … Besides the square piers which support it, there are, on the right and left sides, four porphyry columns, each of which is worth ten times the amount of the tribute (Kharaj) from Misr. These columns were brought from the capital of Misr, along the Nile, to Iskanderiyyeh, and there embarked on rafts …
… On the four piers are written, "Allah, Mohammed, Abu Bekr, 'Omar, 'Osman, 'Ali, Hasan, and Hosein." …
… This mosque has four minarets, the galleries of which are ten in number, as a record that Sultan Suleiman Khan was the tenth Sultan of the House of 'Osman.

paragraphs: … Neither doth any study Mathematics or Physic, which is in any hope of the Ethic glory, but such as want of wit or means hath deterred from studies more sublime. Contrariwise, that Ethic Science is the Ladder of China felicity. Confucius brought into order the Books of four former Philosophers, and wrote a fifth himself, which five Books he called Doctrines: in which are contained Moral and Politic Rules, Examples of the Ancients, Rites and Sacrifices, divers Poems also and the like. … And the ancient Kings enacted that they which profess Learning, should take the foundations of their Learning from those Books … In this Science are three Degrees bestowed on them which offer themselves to be examined and are judged meet. That Examination is almost wholly in Writing. …

… In this [first] Examination every one is admitted, perhaps four or 5000 assembled to that purpose. The second is by the four Governors of the City (for none are admitted to Government but the Learned) which present out of all that number 200 of the better Writers to the Tihio, and he in a third Examination chooseth 20 or 30 of the best, which he entitleth Bachelors … in all places they are much respected as in a rank above the vulgar Citizens, and enjoy also divers Privileges …

… In every Mother City is a huge Palace built for this purpose, compassed with high walls, with many stations for the Examiners separate from noise; and four thousand Cells or Studies besides in the midst of the Palace, wherein is a stool and table for one man, that none may see or confer with any other. … When the Bachelors come to the Palace, they are thoroughly searched whether they have any Book or Writing with them …

… They use to grant at the same times and places … Titles (in the Moon following) to Military Professors, but with less pomp, because Soldiery is of no such reckoning with them, and few stand for them.

paragraphs: There has been arable land from time immemorial, and taxation in consequence. Taxes are of extreme importance:—the State depends on them to meet all its expenses: in the nature of the case they should be collected by the State from the people, and rendered by the people to the State. In all history, which Dynasty has not thus levied them? Besides, the fact is, these taxes are not for the private uses of the Government, but are used for you people. For example, they are used to sustain the numerous officials, that they may look after you; and to support numerous troops, that they may protect you. … there are cities, canals, embankments, boats, and granaries to be built and kept in repair—uses without number; all beyond question simply applying your taxes to promote your interests: never has the State oppressed the people for its own gratification.

From the establishment of Our Dynasty, there has been a fixed amount of taxes to be rendered. Those who exact over and above the fixed amount, and those who, acting in another's name, serve their own ends, shall one and all be got rid of: not a thread or a hair too much is to be collected from you. … Now, since the State unquestionably takes special care of you, you must reciprocate: it is your bounden duty to look on the business of the State as far more pressing than your own.
P9.attribution: The Sacred Edict, sixteen moral maxims issued by the Kangxi Emperor of Qing China in 1670; this passage is from the explanation of the fourteenth maxim, "Pay taxes, and so avoid being pressed for payment," written by his son, the Yongzheng Emperor, in 1724 and later rewritten in everyday Chinese, in a version credited to the Qing official Wang Youpu, so that it could be read aloud to the public

paragraphs: These excursions [to a small hunting castle at Versailles] of Louis XIV. by degrees gave birth to those immense buildings he erected at Versailles; and their convenience for a numerous court, so different from the apartments at Saint-Germain, led him to take up his abode there entirely …

The frequent fetes, the private promenades at Versailles, the journeys, were means on which the King seized in order to distinguish or mortify the courtiers, and thus render them more assiduous in pleasing him. …

… He looked to the right and to the left, not only upon rising but upon going to bed, at his meals, in passing through his apartments, or his gardens of Versailles, where alone the courtiers were allowed to follow him; he saw and noticed everybody; not one escaped him, not even those who hoped to remain unnoticed. He marked well all absentees from the Court, found out the reason of their absence, and never lost an opportunity of acting towards them as the occasion might seem to justify. With some of the courtiers (the most distinguished), it was a demerit not to make the Court their ordinary abode; with others 'twas a fault to come but rarely; for those who never or scarcely ever came it was certain disgrace.
items.attribution: Louis de Rouvroy, Duke of Saint-Simon, French noble who lived at the court of Versailles, Memoirs, written in the 1740s about the reign of Louis XIV (ruled 1643–1715)
items.translation: Translated by Bayle St. John (1857); adapted

paragraphs: … Rulers then act as the ministers of God and as his lieutenants on earth. It is through them that God exercises his empire. … Consequently, as we have seen, the royal throne is not the throne of a man, but the throne of God himself. …

It appears from all this that the person of the king is sacred, and that to attack him in any way is sacrilege. … Kings should be guarded as holy things, and whosoever neglects to protect them is worthy of death. …

But kings, although their power comes from on high, as has been said, should not regard themselves as masters of that power to use it at their pleasure; … they must employ it with fear and self-restraint, as a thing coming from God and of which God will demand an account.

paragraphs: … Here are many shops of artificers, and merchants, and especially of such as weave linen and cotton cloth. And hither do the Barbary merchants bring cloth of Europe. … The inhabitants, and especially strangers there residing, are exceeding rich, insomuch, that the king that now is, married both his daughters unto two rich merchants. …

… Corn, cattle, milk, and butter this region yieldeth in great abundance: but salt is very scarce here; for it is brought hither by land from Tegaza, which is five hundred miles distant. When I myself was here, I saw one camel's load of salt sold for 80 ducats. The rich king of Tombuto hath many plates and sceptres of gold, some whereof weigh 1300 pounds: and he keeps a magnificent and well furnished court. …

… He hath always three thousand horsemen, and a great number of footmen that shoot poisoned arrows, attending upon him. They have often skirmishes with those that refuse to pay tribute, and so many as they take, they sell unto the merchants of Tombuto. Here are very few horses bred, and the merchants and courtiers keep certain little nags which they use to travel upon: but their best horses are brought out of Barbary. …

… Here are great store of doctors, judges, priests, and other learned men, that are bountifully maintained at the king's cost and charges. And hither are brought divers manuscripts or written books out of Barbary, which are sold for more money than any other merchandise.

paragraphs: The Romanists have, with great adroitness, drawn three walls round themselves, with which they have hitherto protected themselves, so that no one could reform them, whereby all Christendom has fallen terribly. Firstly, if pressed by the temporal power, they have affirmed and maintained that the temporal power has no jurisdiction over them, but on the contrary that the spiritual power is above the temporal. Secondly, if it were proposed to admonish them with the Scriptures, they objected that no one may interpret the Scriptures but the Pope. Thirdly, if they are threatened with a Council, they pretend that no one may call a Council but the Pope. …

… It has been devised, that the Pope, bishops, priests and monks are called the Spiritual Estate; Princes, lords, artificers and peasants, are the Temporal Estate; which is a very fine, hypocritical device. … That all Christians are truly of the Spiritual Estate, and there is no difference among them, save of office alone. … Thus we are all consecrated as priests by baptism …
P12.attribution: Martin Luther, German religious reformer, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, 1520

paragraphs: In Gobindwal, which is on the river Biyah (Beas), there was a Hindu named Arjun, in the garments of sainthood and sanctity, so much so that he had captured many of the simple-hearted of the Hindus, and even of the ignorant and foolish followers of Islam, by his ways and manners, and they had loudly sounded the drum of his holiness. They called him Guru, and from all sides stupid people crowded to worship and manifest complete faith in him. For three or four generations (of spiritual successors) they had kept this shop warm. Many times it occurred to me to put a stop to this vain affair or to bring him into the assembly of the people of Islam.

At last when Khusrau* passed along this road this insignificant fellow proposed to wait upon him. Khusrau happened to halt at the place where he was, and he came out and did homage to him. … When this came to my ears and I clearly understood his folly, I ordered them to produce him and handed over his houses, dwelling-places, and children to Murtaza Khan, and having confiscated his property commanded that he should be put to death.

paragraphs: … crowds of learned men from all nations, and sages of various religions and sects came to the Court, and were honoured with private conversations. After enquiries and investigations, which were their only business and occupation day and night, they would talk about profound points of science, the subtleties of revelation, the curiosities of history, and the wonders of nature … everything that pleased him [Akbar], he picked and chose from any one except a Moslem, and anything that was against his disposition, and ran counter to his wishes he thought fit to reject and cast aside. From childhood to manhood, and from manhood to his declining years the Emperor had combined in himself various phases from various religions and opposite sectarian beliefs …

… this conviction took form, like an engraving upon a stone, that there are wise men to be found and ready at hand in all religions, and men of asceticism, and recipients of revelation and workers of miracles among all nations, and that the Truth is an inhabitant of every place: and that consequently how could it be right to consider it as confined to one religion or creed, and that, one which had only recently made its appearance and had not as yet endured a thousand years! …

paragraphs: The reverence and love of the people for the king, … are incredible, as they worship him not as a king, but as a god, on account of his descent from the line of Ali, the great object of their veneration. Those who are in sickness or hardships do not call to aid the name of God so much as that of the king, making vows to present him with some gift, and some go to kiss the doors of the palace, that house being considered fortunate which is able to get some cloth or shawl from the king, or else some water in which he has washed his hands, which they consider a preventive of fever. …
… not only the people, but his own sons and the sultans speak to him as if they could not find epithets worthy of such greatness, saying, "Thou art the living faith, and in thee we believe." …

… It is true that in the city of Tauris he is not held in such veneration as in the other places, for which reason it is said that he has left it and gone to stay at Casin, seeing that he was not esteemed there as he wished.

practice.stem: Busbecq's statement that "the only obstacle is Persia" is best explained by which of the following?

options.A: Persia had joined the Habsburgs in a formal alliance against the Ottomans.
options.B: Persian merchants controlled the silk trade that Ottoman cities depended on.
options.C: The rivalry with the Safavids forced the Ottomans to guard their eastern border.
options.D: Persian grain exports were needed to feed the Ottoman armies in Europe.

practice.explanation: The Ottoman and Safavid empires were rivals for most of the 1500s. When the sultan marched west into Europe, he had to worry about a Safavid attack in the east. Busbecq hoped this would keep the Ottomans busy.

whyNot.A: Habsburg and Persian rulers sometimes exchanged envoys, but they had no real alliance. Busbecq points to Persia's position behind the sultan, not to a treaty.
whyNot.B: Persian silk did reach Ottoman markets, but Busbecq's point is military: Persia lies behind the sultan as he marches west.
whyNot.D: Busbecq says the Persians burn their own crops to starve invaders. They were enemies, not suppliers.

practice.hint: Where is Persia compared with the Ottoman Empire? Why would a sultan heading west worry about it?

practice.stem: Rüstem's comment in the last paragraph suggests that Ottoman leaders

options.A: were willing to ally with Christian rulers against the Safavids
options.B: saw their war with Persia as a quarrel over land, like Spain and France
options.C: hoped to win the Safavids over to Sunni Islam by peaceful teaching
options.D: viewed the Shi'a Safavids as worse enemies of the faith than Christians

practice.explanation: Rüstem says the Ottomans "hate the Persians worse" than Christians. The Ottomans were Sunni Muslims, and the Safavids made Shi'a Islam their state religion. His words show how bitter the rivalry between the two dynasties had become.

whyNot.A: Rüstem compares how much the Ottomans hate each group. He does not offer to join Christians in a war.
whyNot.B: That is Busbecq's idea. Rüstem rejects it: "It is quite a different case."
whyNot.C: Rüstem speaks of hatred, not of peaceful teaching.

practice.hint: Busbecq compares the Ottoman–Persian war to a war between Spain and France. Does Rüstem agree?

practice.stem: Busbecq's comparison of Ottoman and Christian armies most strongly supports which claim?

options.A: The Ottomans' discipline and resources gave them an edge over European armies.
options.B: Ottoman victories came mainly from their larger numbers of firearms.
options.C: European armies were stronger but lacked the will to fight the Ottomans.
options.D: The Ottomans owed their success mainly to their alliance with France.

practice.explanation: Busbecq contrasts Ottoman "order, discipline, thrift" with Christian "luxurious habits" and "greedy generals." He fears the Ottoman way will win. A large, well-run standing army helped the Ottomans expand.

whyNot.B: Busbecq credits "order, discipline, thrift," wealth, and experience. He does not mention guns in this passage.
whyNot.C: Busbecq says the Christian side has "exhausted resources" and "a raw and insubordinate soldiery." He does not think it is stronger.
whyNot.D: France and the Ottomans did cooperate against the Habsburgs, but Busbecq explains Ottoman strength by their own qualities.

practice.hint: Make two lists: what Busbecq says is on "their side" and what is on "ours."

practice.stem: The painting best illustrates which of the following developments in the period 1450–1750?

options.A: Mughal rulers relied on European gunners to aim and fire their cannons.
options.B: Rajput rulers adopted firearms to defend their forts against the Mughals.
options.C: Land-based empires used heavy artillery to capture fortified places.
options.D: Mughal armies used elephants instead of oxen to move their heavy guns.

practice.explanation: Big cannons could smash walls that had held out for centuries. The Mughals, like the Ottomans and Safavids, used gunpowder weapons to conquer new lands. Historians sometimes call these states "gunpowder empires."

whyNot.A: The painting shows no Europeans. Mughal gunners and workers move and fire the guns.
whyNot.B: The attribution says this was an attack on Ranthambhor, so the cannons belong to the attackers, not the defenders.
whyNot.D: The painting shows oxen, not elephants, pulling the guns.

practice.hint: What are the oxen pulling, and where are the men taking it?

practice.stem: The painting was most likely made in order to

options.A: record the methods of moving artillery so officers could learn them
options.B: celebrate the emperor's military strength
options.C: show sympathy for the workers and animals forced to labor in war
options.D: show the hardships of a defeat suffered by Akbar's army

practice.explanation: Akbar ordered the Akbarnama to tell the story of his reign, and his court painters filled it with scenes of his armies' power. Books like this helped show that he deserved to rule.

whyNot.A: The painting shows a dramatic scene, not step-by-step instructions. It was made for a royal history book.
whyNot.C: The painting shows the army's power. Nothing in it criticizes the hard labor.
whyNot.D: Akbar's army took Ranthambhor in 1569, and a history made for Akbar would not show his army defeated.

practice.hint: Who would see an illustrated history made at Akbar's court? What would the emperor want them to think?

practice.stem: The siege shown in the painting is most similar to which of the following?

options.A: The Ming emperors' rebuilding of the Great Wall to keep out Mongol raiders
options.B: The Safavid army's reliance on Kizilbash cavalry charges at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514
options.C: Russian Cossacks' building of small wooden forts as they moved across Siberia
options.D: The Ottoman use of giant cannons to break the walls of Constantinople in 1453

practice.explanation: In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II used huge cannons to batter the walls of Constantinople. Like Akbar at Ranthambhor, he used artillery to take a strong fortress and expand his empire.

whyNot.A: The Great Wall was a defense against raiders. The painting shows an army hauling cannons to attack a fortress.
whyNot.B: The Kizilbash fought on horseback with few guns, and they lost to Ottoman cannons at Chaldiran.
whyNot.C: Cossack forts helped Russia hold land, but they were not cannon attacks on a strong fortress.

practice.hint: What kind of weapon is being moved, and what is it going to be used against?

practice.stem: The reforms described in the first paragraph were intended mainly to

options.A: reduce the shah's need for tribal chiefs and strengthen royal control
options.B: reward the Kizilbash chiefs with larger forces for their loyalty
options.C: prepare Persia's army to invade the Mughal lands in India
options.D: meet the Sherley brothers' demand for a European-style army

practice.explanation: The Kizilbash horsemen "would obey none but their chiefs," so the shah could not fully command his own army. By paying new troops and choosing their officers himself, Abbas built forces loyal to him.

whyNot.B: Abbas did the opposite. He "halved the numbers of the tribal contingents."
whyNot.C: Sykes says the new army was built to "meet that of Turkey," the Ottomans, not to invade India.
whyNot.D: The Sherleys helped train troops, but the shah's own commander-in-chief, Allah Verdi Beg, led the army.

practice.hint: Whom did the Kizilbash obey? Whom did the new troops obey?

practice.stem: Sykes's claim that the changes happened "mainly through the initiative of our fellow-countrymen" most likely reflects

options.A: Persian court chronicles that gave the Sherleys credit for Abbas's victories
options.B: evidence that the Sherley brothers commanded the Persian army in battle
options.C: letters from Shah Abbas thanking England's queen for military help
options.D: his point of view as a British officer who stressed the role of Englishmen

practice.explanation: Sykes was a British officer writing for British readers in 1915. He gives the English brothers much of the credit, even though Shah Abbas and his commanders led the changes. A historian would check Persian sources too.

whyNot.A: Nothing in the passage shows Persian writers giving the Sherleys this credit.
whyNot.B: Sykes names Allah Verdi Beg as commander-in-chief. The Sherleys were advisers.
whyNot.C: The passage mentions no such letters. The Sherleys came as private adventurers.

practice.hint: Who are "our fellow-countrymen"? Who is writing?

practice.stem: Shah Abbas's new paid army was most similar to which of the following?

options.A: Mughal assignments of tax revenue to Rajput nobles who kept commanding their own troops
options.B: The Ottoman Janissaries, salaried infantry who were loyal to the sultan
options.C: Russia's use of Cossack bands who served the tsar in return for land and plunder
options.D: The Ming army's hereditary military families, who passed service from father to son

practice.explanation: Both the Janissaries and Abbas's new troops were paid by the ruler and served him directly. Rulers built such armies so they did not have to depend on nobles or tribal chiefs.

whyNot.A: That system depended on local chiefs and their followers, like the Kizilbash chiefs Abbas was trying to weaken.
whyNot.C: Cossacks were semi-independent bands, not troops paid and officered by the ruler.
whyNot.D: Hereditary soldier families served by birth. Abbas's new troops were paid and appointed by the crown.

practice.hint: Compare how each ruler recruited and paid his troops.

practice.stem: The first paragraph best illustrates which of the following developments?

options.A: Russia's conquest of lands along the Baltic Sea from the kingdom of Sweden
options.B: Russia's expansion southeast along the Volga River and east into western Siberia
options.C: Russia's conquest of the Crimean Khanate on the coast of the Black Sea
options.D: Russia's loss of the Volga lands of Kazan and Astrakhan to the Crimean Tatars

practice.explanation: Ivan IV conquered the khanates of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556) on the Volga River. Soon after, Russians began pushing across Siberia. By the mid-1600s Russian lands reached the Pacific Ocean.

whyNot.A: Russia won Baltic lands later, under Peter the Great. Fletcher names Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia.
whyNot.C: Russia did not take Crimea until 1783. Fletcher names Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia.
whyNot.D: Fletcher says these lands were "won from the Tartar." Russia gained them; it did not lose them.

practice.hint: Find the places Ivan won. In which directions are they from Moscow?

practice.stem: The methods described in the second paragraph show that the Russian state tried to

options.A: win conquered peoples' loyalty by letting them choose their own local leaders
options.B: convert the native peoples to Orthodox Christianity before taxing them
options.C: keep conquered peoples under control with settlers and outside officials
options.D: rule through native princes who paid tribute but kept their own armies

practice.explanation: Fletcher says the tsar settled Russians among the native peoples, appointed Russian officials, split the land into small pieces, and taxed the people heavily. He presents each step as a way to keep the conquered peoples weak and under Moscow's control.

whyNot.A: Fletcher says the officials were "of his own Russe people" and were changed often.
whyNot.B: Fletcher says nothing about religion. Every method he lists is about control and taxes.
whyNot.D: The tsar made sure the people had "neither armour nor money," so they kept no armies.

practice.hint: List Fletcher's four methods. What do they have in common?

practice.stem: Russian expansion into Siberia, described in the passage, was driven mainly by

options.A: the search for silver mines like those the Spanish found in America
options.B: demand for valuable furs that could be taxed and sold abroad
options.C: a need for new farmland to feed Moscow's growing population
options.D: the search for a northern sea route to trade with China

practice.explanation: Siberia's forests were full of sable, fox, and other fur animals. Russian traders, Cossacks, and soldiers moved east, built forts, and forced native peoples to pay tribute in furs, which sold for high prices in Europe and Asia.

whyNot.A: Russia found little silver in Siberia in this period. Furs were the main prize.
whyNot.C: Some Russians did farm in southern Siberia, but valuable furs were the main early prize.
whyNot.D: The push across Siberia went overland along rivers, and its main prize was furs, not a sea route.

practice.hint: What could Siberia offer that buyers in Europe and Asia would pay high prices for?

practice.stem: The reforms described in the passage were part of Peter's broader effort to

options.A: strengthen the Orthodox Church's power over Russian society
options.B: modernize Russia by adopting Western European customs and ideas
options.C: protect old Russian customs from Western European influence
options.D: win the support of the boyars by respecting their traditions

practice.explanation: After touring Western Europe in 1697–1698, Peter wanted Russia to look and act like the powers of the West. Shaving beards and wearing Western clothes were public signs of this change. He also built a new army, a navy, and a new capital, St. Petersburg.

whyNot.A: Priests spread opposition to the reforms, and Peter later put the Church under a council he controlled.
whyNot.C: Peter did the reverse. He ordered "the French fashion" in place of old Russian dress.
whyNot.D: Peter forced the boyars to give up their traditional dress.

practice.hint: Where had Peter traveled just before these reforms, and what did he admire there?

practice.stem: Peter's efforts to Westernize Russia, such as the reforms in the passage, contributed most directly to

options.A: Russia's rise as a major European power after defeating Sweden
options.B: the freeing of Russia's serfs to work in new factories
options.C: Russia's conquest of Constantinople and the Black Sea straits
options.D: a decline in the tsar's power over the boyars and the other nobles

practice.explanation: Peter also changed Russia's army, government, and taxes. His new army and navy defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War (1700–1721). Russia gained land on the Baltic Sea, where Peter built St. Petersburg. Russia was now one of Europe's great powers.

whyNot.B: Serfdom grew stronger under Peter, and many new factories used serf labor. Serfdom ended in 1861.
whyNot.C: Peter fought the Ottomans but did not take Constantinople. His lasting gains were on the Baltic.
whyNot.D: Peter made the tsar more powerful. He forced nobles to serve the state and obey his orders.

practice.hint: What war did Peter's new army and navy fight in the early 1700s?

practice.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the passage as evidence of how Russians reacted to Peter's reforms?

options.A: Rousset lived far from Russia and does not say how he learned of these reactions.
options.B: Rousset describes the reactions of older Russians but not of younger ones.
options.C: Rousset leaves out the role of priests in stirring up opposition.
options.D: Rousset does not explain what the tsar's new rules required.

practice.explanation: A limitation is a reason to be careful with a source. Rousset wrote from the Netherlands and does not name his sources here; in fact, he never visited Russia. Historians would check his account against Russian decrees, letters, and other records.

whyNot.B: Rousset also says the young men "followed the new custom with the more readiness."
whyNot.C: Rousset says the complaints "came from the priests."
whyNot.D: Rousset describes both the beard tax and the order to wear "the French fashion."

practice.hint: Where did Rousset live, and does he say where his information came from?

practice.stem: Evliya's description best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: Ottoman wealth came mainly from trade with Western Europe.
options.B: Rulers used monumental architecture to show their power and piety.
options.C: Religious buildings were paid for mainly by Sufi orders, not the sultan.
options.D: Ottoman builders depended on Byzantine Christian masters to design mosques.

practice.explanation: Suleiman gathered thousands of master builders and used costly stone brought from as far as Egypt. A grand mosque showed the sultan's wealth and his devotion to Islam, which helped make his rule seem rightful.

whyNot.A: The passage measures the columns' value in tribute from Egypt. It says nothing about trade with Europe.
whyNot.C: Evliya says Sultan Suleiman built the mosque and gathered its builders.
whyNot.D: Evliya says the masters came from "the dominions of the house of 'Osman," and the Byzantine Empire had ended in 1453.

practice.hint: Why would a sultan want everyone in his capital to see a building like this?

practice.stem: Evliya's comparison of the mosque's dome with the dome of Aya Sofiyah most likely reflects

options.A: the Ottomans' rejection of older building styles as un-Islamic
options.B: the influence of Persian architects whom the Ottomans brought from Tabriz
options.C: Ottoman builders' lack of skill in raising large domes before Suleiman's reign
options.D: the Ottomans' wish to match or surpass the Byzantine past of their capital

practice.explanation: The Ottomans conquered Constantinople, the Byzantine capital, in 1453 and made it their own capital. Hagia Sophia was its most famous building. A dome to rival it helped present the Ottomans as worthy heirs of the city's earlier rulers.

whyNot.A: Comparing the domes shows that the Ottomans admired the older building and wanted to rival it, not reject it.
whyNot.B: Some artisans did come from Tabriz after 1514, but Evliya compares the dome with Aya Sofiyah, not with Persian work.
whyNot.C: Ottoman builders had raised large domes before, and Evliya stresses the skill of the "perfect masters" Suleiman gathered.

practice.hint: When was Aya Sofiyah built, and who ruled the city before the Ottomans?

practice.stem: The names written on the four piers most directly reflect

options.A: the sultan's claim to be descended from the Prophet's family
options.B: Suleiman's effort to win Shi'a subjects by honoring 'Ali and his sons
options.C: the sultan's wish to honor Osman, the founder of his own dynasty
options.D: the Ottoman dynasty's identity as Sunni Muslims

practice.explanation: Sunni Muslims honor all of the first four caliphs. Shi'a Muslims believe 'Ali should have led first and do not accept the three caliphs before him as rightful leaders. Placing Abu Bekr, 'Omar, and 'Osman on the piers showed the Ottomans' Sunni faith.

whyNot.A: The Ottomans did not claim descent from Muhammad. It was the Safavids who claimed descent from 'Ali.
whyNot.B: The piers also honor Abu Bekr, 'Omar, and 'Osman, whom Shi'a Muslims do not accept as rightful caliphs. That is a Sunni list.
whyNot.C: The glossary explains that this 'Osman is the caliph Uthman, one of the first four caliphs.

practice.hint: Look at which names are on the piers. What religious tradition does that list fit?

practice.stem: The huge halo behind Jahangir's head was most likely meant to

options.A: show that the emperor had become a Christian
options.B: show that the emperor's authority came from God
options.C: celebrate the emperor's victory over the rulers shown below him
options.D: honor the Hindu sun god whom the emperor worshiped

practice.explanation: Mughal artists drew on Persian, Indian, and European art to show royal power. Mughal writers described the emperor as shining with a light from God, and the halo shows Jahangir glowing with that light.

whyNot.A: Halos appear in Christian art, but Jahangir stayed a Muslim. Mughal artists borrowed the halo to show God's blessing.
whyNot.C: No battle is shown, and the kings below are visitors, not prisoners.
whyNot.D: The sun and moon praise the emperor's own power. The painting does not show him worshiping a Hindu god.

practice.hint: In art, what does a glowing circle around a person's head usually mean?

practice.stem: Bichitr's choice to show Jahangir handing a book to a Sufi shaikh while kings wait below was most likely meant to

options.A: show that the emperor took orders from Sufi leaders in matters of state
options.B: celebrate the emperor's alliances with the Ottoman sultan and the English king
options.C: present the emperor as a pious Muslim ruler who valued holy men above worldly power
options.D: warn Sufi leaders that the emperor would take control of their shrines

practice.explanation: Mughal emperors honored Sufi saints, such as the Chishti saints of Ajmer. By showing Jahangir favoring a holy man over kings, the painting presents him as both a mighty ruler and a devout Muslim.

whyNot.A: Jahangir gives the shaikh a gift from his throne. He honors the shaikh but does not take orders from him.
whyNot.B: The kings stand below and wait. The painting ranks them beneath the holy man instead of celebrating them as allies.
whyNot.D: The emperor is giving the shaikh a gift, a sign of respect, not a threat.

practice.hint: To whom does Jahangir turn, and who is left waiting?

practice.stem: Jahangir's use of art to strengthen his authority was most similar to

options.A: Louis XIV's building of the palace of Versailles to display royal glory
options.B: Martin Luther's use of printed pamphlets with woodcut pictures to attack the pope
options.C: Jesuit missionaries' use of European paintings to teach Christianity in China
options.D: Safavid potters' copying of Chinese porcelain designs to sell to European buyers

practice.explanation: Rulers in many empires used art and buildings to look powerful and blessed. Jahangir used paintings like this one, and Louis XIV built a huge palace. Both wanted subjects and rivals to see their greatness.

whyNot.B: Luther used pictures to attack the pope's power, not to build up a ruler's own power.
whyNot.C: The Jesuits used art to spread their religion, not to praise a ruler.
whyNot.D: The potters made art to sell, not to show a ruler's greatness.

practice.hint: For each choice, ask: Who made or ordered the art, and whose power was it meant to build up?

practice.stem: The system Ricci describes best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: Recruiting officials through exams on Confucian learning
options.B: Choosing officials from families that held their posts by birth
options.C: Training enslaved boys from conquered peoples to serve as officials
options.D: Selling government offices to wealthy merchant families

practice.explanation: Ming China chose many of its officials through written exams on the Confucian classics. Passing earned a degree, respect, and a chance at government jobs. The exams gave the emperor educated officials who owed their posts to the state.

whyNot.B: Ricci says none are admitted to government "but the Learned," who earn degrees by exam.
whyNot.C: That was the Ottoman devshirme. Ricci describes free men taking written exams.
whyNot.D: Ricci describes degrees won by examination, not offices bought with money.

practice.hint: According to Ricci, who is allowed into government?

practice.stem: Compared with the Ottoman devshirme, the Ming system described in the passage placed more emphasis on

options.A: hereditary claims to government offices held by noble families
options.B: military training for boys raised in the ruler's household
options.C: recommendations from powerful local families and officials
options.D: performance on written exams in classical learning

practice.explanation: The Ming exams tested knowledge of the Chinese classics. The devshirme forced selected Christian boys into Ottoman service, where they trained as soldiers or palace officials. Neither was its empire's only path into government.

whyNot.A: Ricci describes competitive exams. Offices were not inherited.
whyNot.B: That describes the devshirme, which trained boys in the sultan's household. Ricci says "Soldiery is of no such reckoning" in China.
whyNot.C: Ricci says candidates had to pass written exams. He does not describe recommendations.

practice.hint: How did each empire find its future officials?

practice.stem: Ricci's detailed description of the exams was most likely written for

options.A: Chinese officials who needed rules for running the exams
options.B: European readers who wanted to know how China was governed
options.C: Ming emperors who were planning to reform the exams
options.D: the pope, to argue that Jesuits should run China's schools

practice.explanation: Ricci's account was printed in Latin and then in English, so it was meant mainly for European readers. Europeans were curious about the huge empire that missionaries and traders were reaching.

whyNot.A: Chinese officials already knew the system. Ricci explains it as something new and strange.
whyNot.C: Ricci was a foreign missionary, not an adviser on the exams.
whyNot.D: Ricci describes the Chinese system with respect. He does not argue that Jesuits should replace it.

practice.hint: Look at the attribution. In what languages was this account published?

practice.stem: The passage was most likely intended to

options.A: announce a new tax to pay for the emperor's wars on the frontier
options.B: explain why the emperor was forgiving unpaid taxes in famine years
options.C: warn local officials that the emperor would raise tax rates
options.D: persuade ordinary people that paying taxes was a duty that helped them

practice.explanation: These lessons were read aloud to ordinary people. The passage says that taxes pay for officials, soldiers, canals, and granaries that protect the people. In return, people should pay willingly.

whyNot.A: The passage says the tax amount had been fixed since the dynasty began. It announces no new tax.
whyNot.B: The passage urges people to pay their taxes, not to wait for them to be forgiven.
whyNot.C: The passage promises that "not a thread or a hair too much" will be taken.

practice.hint: Who was supposed to hear this passage? What did the government want them to do?

practice.stem: Qing taxes were collected largely in silver, as late Ming taxes had been. This practice depended most directly on

options.A: the discovery of rich new silver mines in northern China
options.B: a ban on foreign trade that kept silver inside China
options.C: large inflows of silver from Japan and Spanish America
options.D: silver paid by Russian merchants trading furs at the border

practice.explanation: China sold silk, porcelain, and tea to the world and was paid in silver. Much of it came from Japan. Much more came from Spanish mines in the Americas, by way of Manila and other trade routes. This flow let Ming and Qing rulers collect taxes in silver.

whyNot.A: China had few large silver mines of its own. Most of its silver came from abroad.
whyNot.B: Silver came into China through foreign trade. A trade ban would have cut off the supply.
whyNot.D: Trade with Russia was small. Far more silver came by sea from Japan and the Americas.

practice.hint: Where did most of the world's silver come from in the 1500s and 1600s?

practice.stem: Which of the following claims does the passage best support?

options.A: Qing rulers let each province set its own tax rates.
options.B: Qing rulers said the state cared for the people, who owed it loyalty.
options.C: The Qing government spent most of its taxes on the emperor's palaces and court.
options.D: Qing rulers believed taxes should rise as the population grew.

practice.explanation: The passage lists the ways taxes "promote your interests" and says the people "must reciprocate." This fits the Confucian idea that a ruler should care for his people like a father, and the people should be loyal.

whyNot.A: The passage says there has been "a fixed amount of taxes" since the dynasty began.
whyNot.C: The passage says taxes are "not for the private uses of the Government."
whyNot.D: The passage stresses a fixed amount of taxes. In 1712 the Kangxi Emperor had in fact frozen the head tax.

practice.hint: Find the word "reciprocate." What does the passage say each side owes the other?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 calls royal power sinful; Source 2 defends the nobles' right to resist a king who abuses power.
options.B: Source 1 shows how Louis XIV controlled nobles; Source 2 gives a religious reason for royal power.
options.C: Both sources argue that kings must share power with an elected assembly.
options.D: Both sources describe how Louis XIV raised taxes to pay for Versailles.

practice.explanation: Saint-Simon shows a practical way the king kept nobles weak: keeping them at court where he could watch them. Bossuet explains why the king deserved such power: his throne is "the throne of God himself."

whyNot.A: Saint-Simon describes the king's methods without calling them sinful, and Bossuet says kings are sacred.
whyNot.C: Neither source mentions an assembly. Bossuet says kings answer to God.
whyNot.D: Neither source discusses taxes.

practice.hint: State each writer's main point in a few words before comparing them.

practice.stem: Louis XIV's methods described in Source 1 were most directly intended to

options.A: weaken the independent power of nobles by keeping them under the king's eye
options.B: train nobles as professional army officers loyal to the king
options.C: persuade the nobles to give up their old exemptions from paying the royal taxes
options.D: give nobles a voice in royal decisions through an assembly

practice.explanation: Nobles who lived at Versailles competed for the king's favor instead of building power in their own lands. Louis noticed who came and who stayed away, and those who stayed away fell into "certain disgrace."

whyNot.B: Louis did build a professional army, but Saint-Simon describes court life, favors, and disgrace, not military training.
whyNot.C: Saint-Simon does not mention taxes. The nobles stayed free of France's main tax, the taille.
whyNot.D: Louis XIV ruled without calling France's assembly of estates. Saint-Simon shows the king, not the nobles, deciding.

practice.hint: What happened to nobles who did not come to court?

practice.stem: Bossuet's ideas in Source 2 are most similar to which of the following?

options.A: Luther's teaching that baptized Christians share in the priesthood
options.B: The Chinese idea that emperors ruled under the Mandate of Heaven
options.C: The English Parliament's claim that kings must obey the law and share power
options.D: Akbar's invitations to scholars of many faiths to debate at his court

practice.explanation: Bossuet says a king's power comes from God, and God will judge how he uses it. In China, the Mandate of Heaven also said that heaven gave rulers their power and could take it away from bad rulers.

whyNot.A: Luther's idea gives spiritual standing to believers. Bossuet raises the king above everyone.
whyNot.C: Parliament wanted to limit the king's power. Bossuet says the king answers only to God.
whyNot.D: Akbar's debates were about religious ideas, not about where a ruler's power comes from.

practice.hint: Underline the words Bossuet uses to say where a king's power comes from.

practice.stem: Leo's description of Timbuktu's scholars best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: Songhai rulers distrusted the scholars and kept them away from the court.
options.B: Songhai rulers backed Islamic learning, which added to their authority.
options.C: Timbuktu's scholars chose each new Songhai ruler.
options.D: Timbuktu's learning depended on scholars sent from Mamluk Egypt.

practice.explanation: Leo says the ruler paid Muslim scholars and judges. Supporting Islamic learning could win a ruler respect and strengthen his authority. Timbuktu became famous for its books and schools.

whyNot.A: Leo says the scholars are "bountifully maintained at the king's cost," so the king supported them.
whyNot.C: Leo says the king pays the scholars. Nothing shows the scholars choosing kings.
whyNot.D: Leo says books came from Barbary (North Africa). He says nothing about scholars sent from Egypt.

practice.hint: Who pays the learned men? Why would a ruler want to do that?

practice.stem: Leo's description of the king's army best supports which claim?

options.A: The king's army relied mainly on muskets bought from North African merchants.
options.B: The king bred his own war horses in large numbers near Timbuktu.
options.C: The king avoided war and depended on merchants to defend the city.
options.D: The king used cavalry and raids to force neighboring peoples to pay tribute.

practice.explanation: Songhai's rulers kept a strong cavalry force. They raided peoples who refused to pay tribute and sold captives to merchants. Horses from North Africa helped make this army powerful.

whyNot.A: Leo's footmen "shoot poisoned arrows." He mentions no guns.
whyNot.B: Leo says "very few horses" are bred there; the best come from Barbary.
whyNot.C: Leo describes 3,000 horsemen and frequent "skirmishes" with those who refuse tribute.

practice.hint: What does the king's army do to people who refuse to pay tribute?

practice.stem: Leo's account is most useful to historians as evidence of

options.A: the religious beliefs of ordinary farmers in the villages of the Songhai countryside
options.B: how European missionaries viewed Islam in Africa
options.C: trade and court life in West Africa as seen by a North African visitor
options.D: the Songhai rulers' own explanations of their policies

practice.explanation: Leo saw Timbuktu's markets and court for himself. As a visitor from Morocco, he noticed prices, trade goods, and court customs. The passage says little about life in the villages.

whyNot.A: Leo describes the city and the court, not village farmers.
whyNot.B: Leo was a scholar from North Africa, not a European missionary.
whyNot.D: Leo was an outside visitor. He reports what he saw, not the rulers' own words.

practice.hint: Which subjects does this passage describe in detail?

practice.stem: Luther's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: the pope's supporters use false claims of power to block Church reform
options.B: German princes should accept the pope's authority over questions of religion
options.C: monks, nuns, and priests deserve a higher place in society than princes
options.D: peasants should rise up against lords who support the pope in Rome

practice.explanation: Luther says the pope's supporters hid behind "three walls" to avoid reform: that the Church is above rulers, that only the pope can explain the Bible, and that only the pope can call a council. He argues that all baptized Christians are priests, so the clergy are not above everyone else. This opened the way for rulers to reform the Church.

whyNot.B: Luther attacks the claim that "the spiritual power is above the temporal."
whyNot.C: Luther calls the idea of a separate Spiritual Estate "a very fine, hypocritical device."
whyNot.D: Luther speaks to the nobles and asks them to act. He does not call on peasants to revolt.

practice.hint: What are the "three walls," and what does Luther want to do to them?

practice.stem: Luther addressed this work to the German nobility most likely because he

options.A: believed the German nobles had a duty to defend the pope's authority
options.B: wanted the nobles to pay for St. Peter's Basilica
options.C: believed the nobles had already left the Catholic Church
options.D: hoped princes would use their power to reform the Church

practice.explanation: Luther needed protectors. Princes could shield reformers and take charge of churches in their own lands. Frederick the Wise of Saxony did protect Luther after the pope and the emperor condemned him.

whyNot.A: Luther attacks the pope's claims. He wants the nobles to reform the Church, not defend the pope.
whyNot.B: Luther criticized raising money for St. Peter's. He did not ask nobles to pay for it.
whyNot.C: In 1520 the German princes were still Catholic. Luther was trying to win them over.

practice.hint: What could powerful nobles do that a monk could not?

practice.stem: Ideas like those in the passage contributed most directly to

options.A: rulers in northern Europe breaking with Rome and forming state churches
options.B: the reunion of Western Christianity under the pope
options.C: a decline in the control that rulers had over religion within their own lands
options.D: the end of Catholic missions outside Europe

practice.explanation: Many German princes, the kings of Denmark and Sweden, and later the English crown broke with the pope and set up churches under their own control. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let rulers in the Holy Roman Empire choose either Catholicism or Lutheranism for their lands.

whyNot.B: The Reformation divided Western Christianity. It did not reunite it.
whyNot.C: The opposite happened. Protestant rulers took control of the churches in their lands.
whyNot.D: Catholic missions grew. Jesuits and other orders went to Asia and the Americas.

practice.hint: Luther said rulers had a right to reform the Church. What did many rulers then do?

practice.stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by the chart?

options.A: The order's membership fell during the 1600s.
options.B: The order grew faster from 1680 to 1749 than from 1556 to 1615.
options.C: The Jesuit order grew more than tenfold between 1556 and 1615.
options.D: The order had more than 30,000 members by 1749.

practice.explanation: In 1556 the order had about 1,000 members. By 1615 it had 13,112, about thirteen times as many. Growth continued, but more slowly, through 1749.

whyNot.A: Membership rose from 13,112 in 1615 to 17,665 in 1680.
whyNot.B: It added about 4,900 members from 1680 to 1749, but about 12,100 from 1556 to 1615.
whyNot.D: The chart shows 22,589 members in 1749.

practice.hint: Test each choice against the chart. For a choice about how many times bigger, divide one number by the other.

practice.stem: The growth shown in the chart is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Catholic Reformation's response to the spread of Protestantism
options.B: Protestant rulers' closing of monasteries and Catholic religious orders
options.C: the Council of Trent's ban on founding new religious orders
options.D: the spread of Enlightenment ideas in Catholic universities

practice.explanation: The Jesuits were founded in 1540 to defend and spread the Catholic faith. They opened schools, preached, and sent missionaries around the world. Their growth was part of the Catholic Church's answer to Protestant reformers.

whyNot.B: Closing orders would shrink them. The chart shows a Catholic order growing.
whyNot.C: Trent did not ban new orders. The pope had approved the Jesuits in 1540.
whyNot.D: The Enlightenment came mostly after 1700, and many of its writers criticized religious orders.

practice.hint: What was happening to the Catholic Church in Europe in the mid-1500s?

practice.stem: Which additional evidence would best support the argument that the growth shown in the chart helped spread Catholicism beyond Europe?

options.A: Records showing that most early missions in Spanish Mexico were run by Franciscan and Dominican friars
options.B: Records of nobles paying to build Jesuit colleges in European cities
options.C: Records of Jesuit teachers and missionaries working in Asia and the Americas
options.D: Records of Jesuit priests serving as advisers to Catholic kings in Europe

practice.explanation: The chart shows how many Jesuits there were, not where they worked. Records of Jesuits teaching and preaching in places such as Japan, China, India, Brazil, and New France would link the order's growth to the spread of Catholicism.

whyNot.A: Missions run by other religious orders do not show that the Jesuits' growth spread Catholicism.
whyNot.B: Colleges in Europe show growth inside Europe, not the spread of Catholicism beyond it.
whyNot.D: Advising kings in Europe does not show the faith spreading outside Europe.

practice.hint: The chart shows numbers only. What would you need to know to connect those numbers to places outside Europe?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 urges rulers to enforce Islamic law; Source 2 shows a ruler protecting a popular religious teacher.
options.B: Source 1 defends the sacred thread and caste rituals; Source 2 shows a ruler honoring a Sikh guru at court.
options.C: Both sources argue that religious teachers should obey the emperor and stay out of politics.
options.D: Source 1 values inner devotion over ritual; Source 2 shows a ruler treating a growing faith as a threat.

practice.explanation: Nanak's hymns stress kindness, truth, and sincere devotion over outward rituals. Jahangir sees Guru Arjun, a later leader of the community Nanak founded, as a threat and orders his death. Together the sources show a new faith and a ruler's hostile response.

whyNot.A: Nanak says a true Muslim is kind and just; he does not ask rulers to enforce laws. Jahangir orders Arjun's death.
whyNot.B: Nanak asks for a thread made of mercy and truth, not the usual ritual thread. Jahangir has Arjun put to death.
whyNot.C: Neither source says this. Nanak speaks about true faith, and Jahangir writes as an angry ruler.

practice.hint: Sum up each source in a few words. Then test each choice against both summaries.

practice.stem: Jahangir's description of Arjun's followers as "simple-hearted" and "stupid" most likely reflects

options.A: his respect for holy men of many faiths, which he shared with the Sufis
options.B: the policy of tolerance that his father Akbar had followed
options.C: his view that the Sikh movement threatened Islam and his own authority
options.D: his anger that Arjun had refused to pay the Mughal land tax

practice.explanation: Jahangir was angry that Arjun drew Muslim followers and had honored Khusrau, the prince who rebelled. His insulting words show how he saw the Guru: as a dangerous rival to his faith and his throne.

whyNot.A: Jahangir did honor Sufi shaikhs, but here he calls Arjun's following a "vain affair" and orders his death.
whyNot.B: Akbar welcomed teachers of many faiths. Jahangir's words show hostility instead.
whyNot.D: Jahangir says nothing about taxes. He is angry about Arjun's popularity and his support for Khusrau.

practice.hint: Why would an emperor be bothered by a popular religious teacher who had met his rebel son?

practice.stem: Events like the one described in Source 2 contributed most directly to

options.A: the Sikhs' merger with the Chishti Sufi order in the Punjab
options.B: the Sikhs' withdrawal from public life to focus on private prayer
options.C: the Sikhs' growing military tradition to defend their community
options.D: an alliance between the Sikh gurus and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb

practice.explanation: After Arjun's death, his son Guru Hargobind began to keep armed followers. In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, a community of Sikhs pledged to defend their faith. Conflict with Mughal rulers shaped these changes.

whyNot.A: The Sikhs remained a separate community led by their own gurus.
whyNot.B: The opposite happened. Later gurus kept armed followers and took a public role.
whyNot.D: Conflict grew worse. Aurangzeb had the ninth guru, Tegh Bahadur, executed in 1675.

practice.hint: How might a religious community respond after its leader is executed by the state?

practice.stem: Bada'uni's description of Akbar's religious views most likely reflects

options.A: his disapproval of Akbar's openness to faiths other than Islam
options.B: his support for Akbar's plan to make Hinduism the official state religion
options.C: his admiration for Akbar's search for truth among many teachers
options.D: the praise of Akbar's tolerance in Abu'l-Fazl's official history

practice.explanation: Bada'uni complains that Akbar "picked and chose from any one except a Moslem." He believed Islam was the one true faith. His critical history shows how some Muslims at court saw Akbar's policies. Working for the emperor did not mean agreeing with him.

whyNot.B: Akbar did not make Hinduism the state religion, and Bada'uni praises no such plan.
whyNot.C: Bada'uni complains that Akbar "picked and chose from any one except a Moslem." He does not admire it.
whyNot.D: Abu'l-Fazl praised Akbar's policies. Bada'uni complains about them.

practice.hint: Which words show how the writer feels about the emperor's choices?

practice.stem: Akbar's religious policies described in the passage most likely helped him to

options.A: enforce Islamic law more strictly across his empire
options.B: end the influence of Jesuit missionaries at his court
options.C: strengthen the power of Sunni scholars over the emperor
options.D: win the loyalty of an empire where most subjects were not Muslim

practice.explanation: Most of Akbar's subjects were Hindus. By honoring teachers of many faiths, marrying Rajput princesses, and ending the jizya tax on non-Muslims, he gained the support of Hindu nobles and soldiers. This helped hold his empire together.

whyNot.A: That describes Aurangzeb, a later emperor. Bada'uni says Akbar found wise men "in all religions."
whyNot.B: Akbar invited Jesuits to his court to join debates.
whyNot.C: Akbar reduced their power, which is why scholars like Bada'uni were unhappy.

practice.hint: Think about who most of Akbar's subjects were.

practice.stem: Akbar's approach to religion, as described by Bada'uni, was most similar to

options.A: Philip II of Spain's efforts to stamp out Protestantism in the Netherlands
options.B: Louis XIV's decision in 1685 to end the toleration of Protestants in France
options.C: Jahangir's order to execute the Sikh leader Guru Arjun, whom he saw as a rival
options.D: Ottoman sultans letting Christian and Jewish groups run some of their affairs

practice.explanation: The Ottomans let Christian and Jewish communities handle some religious and family matters through their own leaders, as long as they paid taxes and stayed loyal. Like Akbar, they allowed religious diversity to keep peace in a mixed empire.

whyNot.A: Philip II used force to defend Catholicism. Akbar welcomed many faiths.
whyNot.B: In 1685 Louis XIV took away the rights of Protestants in France. That was the opposite of tolerance.
whyNot.C: Jahangir punished a religious leader he saw as a threat. That is the opposite of Akbar's openness.

practice.hint: How did Akbar treat teachers of other religions? Which choice shows a ruler treating other faiths in the same way?

practice.stem: The passage best illustrates which method Safavid rulers used to legitimize their power?

options.A: claiming descent from the Mongol khans, as earlier Persian rulers had
options.B: building grand mosques and squares in their capital
options.C: claiming a sacred status through descent from 'Ali
options.D: winning Venetian support against the Ottomans

practice.explanation: The Safavids claimed descent from 'Ali, whom Shi'a Muslims deeply honor. Many of their followers treated the shah as holy, even seeking water he had washed in. This religious devotion strengthened the shah's power.

whyNot.A: D'Alessandri says the people revere the shah "on account of his descent from the line of Ali," not from the Mongols.
whyNot.B: Later shahs did build in Isfahan, but this passage is about the people's religious devotion to the shah.
whyNot.D: Venice did seek Persian help, but the passage is about how Persians saw their own ruler.

practice.hint: Why does d'Alessandri say the people worship the king?

practice.stem: A historian would most likely question d'Alessandri's explanation of why the shah left Tabriz for Qazvin because

options.A: Ottoman armies had attacked and occupied Tabriz, near the Ottoman border
options.B: Tabriz was the shah's birthplace and the main center of his family's support
options.C: Qazvin was the holy city where the Safavid family's Sufi order began
options.D: Qazvin had been destroyed by the Uzbeks shortly before

practice.explanation: Tabriz lies in the far northwest, close to the Ottoman Empire, and Ottoman armies took it several times in the 1500s. Shah Tahmasp moved his capital east to Qazvin, where it was safer. D'Alessandri repeats a story he heard instead.

whyNot.B: Tahmasp was born near Isfahan, and his family's home base was Ardabil, not Tabriz.
whyNot.C: The Safavid Sufi order began at Ardabil, not Qazvin.
whyNot.D: Qazvin became the Safavid capital and was not destroyed. The main threat came from the Ottomans in the west.

practice.hint: D'Alessandri repeats what "it is said." What other reason might a shah have had for moving his capital in the mid-1500s?

practice.stem: The people's devotion to the shah described in the passage is best explained by

options.A: the shah's conversion of Persia from Shi'a to Sunni Islam
options.B: the shah's lowering of taxes on farmers and the common people
options.C: the Safavids' roots as leaders of a revered Sufi order
options.D: the shah's victories over the Mughals at Kandahar

practice.explanation: Before they ruled Persia, the Safavid family led a Sufi brotherhood at Ardabil. Their Kizilbash followers saw them as holy guides. They kept that respect after Isma'il became shah in 1501.

whyNot.A: The Safavids did the reverse. They made Shi'a Islam Persia's official faith.
whyNot.B: D'Alessandri ties the people's devotion to the shah's descent from 'Ali, not to taxes.
whyNot.D: Safavid armies did fight the Mughals over Kandahar, but battles do not explain why people treated the shah as holy.

practice.hint: How did the Safavid family first gain followers, before they ruled Persia?

exam.title: Unit 3 Practice Exam: Land-Based Empires
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of world history from c. 1450 to c. 1750. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or insulting descriptions of other peoples and religions; these words show the writers' views.

questions.stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following developments in the period c. 1450 to c. 1750?

options.A: Rulers in South Asia depended on cannons and muskets bought from Portuguese traders.
options.B: Armies in South Asia gave up mounted archers in favor of foot soldiers with guns.
