options.C: Rulers of land-based empires combined gunpowder weapons with cavalry to win new lands.
options.D: War elephants allowed large armies to overpower smaller forces armed with guns.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Babur's gunner and guns came with him overland from Central Asia, and he copied an Ottoman way of linking carts. "Firingi" names a style of gun; the passage does not mention the Portuguese.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Babur's mounted turning-parties and archers did much of the fighting. Guns were added to cavalry, not used instead of it.
rationales.C: Correct. Babur's gunners fired from behind carts and shields while his horsemen surrounded the enemy and "rained arrows" on him.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Babur reports that Ibrahim had about 1,000 elephants and a much larger army, yet lost in half a day.

questions.explanation: Babur's win at Panipat in 1526 began the Mughal Empire. Like the Ottomans and Safavids, the Mughals used guns along with older strengths, such as skilled horsemen.

questions.stem: Babur's comments about Ibrahim in the second paragraph were most likely meant to

options.A: show that Ibrahim's army had already been weakened by Safavid attacks before the battle
options.B: explain that Babur won because his own army was larger and better paid
options.C: portray his rival as greedy and unfit to rule, making Babur's conquest seem justified
options.D: argue that hired troops from Hindustan were more loyal than his own soldiers

rationales.A: Incorrect. The passage says nothing about Safavid attacks. Babur blames Ibrahim's own greed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Babur stresses the enemy's size, about 100,000 men. He does not claim that his own army was larger.
rationales.C: Correct. Babur says Ibrahim was "ruled by avarice" and would not share his treasure with his soldiers. This portrays his rival as a poor ruler and makes Babur's conquest seem justified.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Babur does not compare the loyalty of different troops. He criticizes Ibrahim for not rewarding his soldiers.

questions.explanation: Babur wrote his memoir to tell his own story. Showing his enemy as a greedy, careless ruler made his own victory look deserved, even blessed by God.

questions.stem: Babur's methods at Panipat were most similar to which of the following?

options.A: The Ottoman defeat of Safavid horsemen at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514
options.B: The Safavid army's reliance on charges by Kizilbash cavalry in the early 1500s
options.C: Ming China's use of the Great Wall to hold back Mongol horsemen
options.D: The Songhai army's reliance on cavalry and archers in the 1500s

rationales.A: Correct. At Chaldiran, Ottoman cannons and muskets fired from behind linked carts and broke the Safavid cavalry. This is the same "Ottoman fashion" Babur's gunner copied.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Kizilbash horsemen were like Ibrahim's side: a mounted force that faced guns. They lost at Chaldiran.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Great Wall was a fixed defense. Babur used guns, carts, and horsemen to attack and win a battle.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Songhai's army fought with horsemen and arrows and had no guns. Babur combined guns, carts, and horsemen.

questions.explanation: Military ideas spread among the Islamic empires of this period. Ottoman methods reached Babur's army, and the Mughals used them to build an empire in India.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 calls for ending the papacy, while Source 2 says councils should rule the Church instead of the pope.
options.B: Source 1 challenges promises made for purchased pardons, while Source 2 upholds indulgences but condemns abuses.
options.C: Source 1 approves of paying for indulgences to build churches, while Source 2 orders the Church to stop granting them.
options.D: Source 1 is addressed to Catholic bishops, while Source 2 is addressed to the German princes.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Luther questions the pope's use of money but does not call for ending the papacy here. Trent does not place councils above the pope.
rationales.B: Correct. Luther says those who think pardons make them "sure of their own salvation" will be damned. Trent says indulgences must be "retained" but orders "all evil gains" abolished.
rationales.C: Incorrect. It is the reverse. Luther attacks building St. Peter's with poor believers' money, and Trent keeps indulgences.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neither source names these audiences. Luther wrote his theses for a debate at his university, and Trent's decree speaks to the whole Church.

questions.explanation: Luther's attack on indulgences in 1517 started the Protestant Reformation. Years later, the Council of Trent answered the Protestants. It kept indulgences but tried to stop people from selling them for money.

questions.stem: Source 2 was written most directly in response to

options.A: Protestant movements that rejected papal authority and many Catholic practices
options.B: Spanish missionaries' protests against the forced labor of Indigenous peoples in America
options.C: the Ottoman sultans' wars against the Habsburg rulers in central Europe
options.D: the arrival of Jesuit missionaries in Japan and China

rationales.A: Correct. Trent condemns those who call indulgences "useless" and complains that their name is "blasphemed by heretics." Those critics were Protestants.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Missionaries such as Las Casas did protest forced labor in the Americas, but that issue had nothing to do with indulgences.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Ottoman–Habsburg wars were a real threat to Catholic Europe, but this decree is about Church teaching on indulgences.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Jesuits carried Catholic teaching to Asia, but this decree answers critics inside Europe.

questions.explanation: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563. It was the center of the Catholic Reformation, the Church's answer to the Protestant Reformation. It restated Catholic beliefs and set out reforms.

questions.stem: The debate shown in the two sources contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: the reunion of the Catholic and Orthodox churches under the leadership of the pope
options.B: a lasting split in Western Christianity between Catholic and Protestant churches
options.C: a sharp decline in Catholic missionary work outside Europe
options.D: an end to religious wars in Europe by the middle of the 1500s

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Catholic and Orthodox churches stayed separate. This debate was within Western Christianity.
rationales.B: Correct. Trent restated the teachings that Protestants rejected, so the two sides did not reunite. Europe stayed divided into Catholic and Protestant lands.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Catholic missions grew. Jesuits and other orders spread Catholicism in Asia and the Americas.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Religious wars went on long after 1563, including the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).

questions.explanation: Before 1517 most Western Europeans belonged to one church. After the Reformation, much of northern Europe became Protestant while southern Europe stayed Catholic, and both kept spreading their faith.

questions.stem: The dragon designs on the emperor's robe and throne were most likely meant to

options.A: show the Manchu clan symbols the emperor's family had used before conquering China
options.B: honor the Buddhist monasteries that had supported the emperor's family
options.C: record the emperor's conquest of the island of Taiwan
options.D: link the emperor to long-standing Chinese symbols of imperial power

rationales.A: Incorrect. The dragon was an old Chinese symbol of the emperor, used for many centuries before the Manchus.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the portrait points to Buddhist monasteries as the source of the emperor's power.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The portrait shows no battle or place. Dragons stood for the emperor in general, not for one event.
rationales.D: Correct. For many centuries the dragon had stood for the Chinese emperor. A ruler covered in dragons and seated on a dragon throne looked like a true Chinese emperor.

questions.explanation: Rulers often used art to look powerful and rightful. Formal court portraits like this one showed the emperor on the dragon throne, wearing robes in colors and patterns reserved for the imperial family.

questions.stem: The portrait was produced in the context of

options.A: a Ming government effort to end the Manchu threat along its northern border
options.B: Manchu rulers' efforts to win the loyalty of China's Han Chinese majority
options.C: the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, which ended Qing rule in southern China
options.D: a Qing policy that kept Han Chinese out of government offices

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, before Kangxi became emperor in 1661. This is a Qing portrait.
rationales.B: Correct. The Qing were Manchus from the northeast who took Beijing in 1644 and conquered the rest of China over the next decades. Kangxi presented himself as a proper Chinese emperor to win over the Han Chinese.
rationales.C: Incorrect. That revolt by three Han Chinese generals (1673–1681) failed. Kangxi crushed it and kept control of the south.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Qing kept Han Chinese officials and the exam system. Many top offices were shared by a Manchu and a Han official.

questions.explanation: The Qing rulers were Manchus, but most people they ruled were Han Chinese. To be accepted, the Qing kept the Confucian exams, honored Chinese customs, and used Chinese symbols of the emperor, while also keeping Manchu traditions.

questions.stem: The portrait's purpose is most similar to which of the following?

options.A: Luther's use of printed pamphlets to win support for reforming the Church
options.B: Shah Abbas's creation of a paid army loyal to the shah himself
options.C: Jesuit missionaries' use of Western astronomy to win favor at the Qing court
options.D: Mughal emperors' building of grand tombs and mosques such as the Taj Mahal

rationales.A: Incorrect. Luther's pamphlets attacked the pope's power. They were not a ruler's art meant to show his right to rule.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A paid army was a military way to build loyalty, not art or architecture.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Jesuits used science to gain a hearing for their faith, not to glorify the emperor.
rationales.D: Correct. Like the portrait, the Taj Mahal and other Mughal monuments used art and buildings to display the ruler's glory and right to rule.

questions.explanation: Many rulers used art and buildings to show they had the right to rule. Qing portraits, Mughal tombs and mosques, and the palace of Versailles all sent the same message: this ruler is great.

questions.stem: Lybyer's description best illustrates which of the following developments?

options.A: Hereditary nobles gained control of the army and the provinces.
options.B: Merchants bought government offices to raise their social status.
options.C: Rulers trained military and government elites who owed their rise to the ruler.
options.D: Religious scholars replaced military leaders as the chief officials of the state.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Lybyer says the system paid "no regard for ancestry," so it did not rely on hereditary nobles.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The recruits did not buy their posts. They were chosen and trained for their ability.
rationales.C: Correct. Lybyer says the system took slaves and farm boys and made them generals, governors, and ministers. They owed their careers to the sultan.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The system produced soldiers and generals as well as scholars, and the army stayed central to Ottoman power.

questions.explanation: Through the devshirme, Ottoman officials forcibly took boys from Christian families, mostly in the Balkans. The boys were made Muslims and trained to be Janissaries or officials. With no noble families to back them, they depended on the sultan.

questions.stem: Ottoman sultans used the system Lybyer describes mainly in order to

options.A: convert the empire's Christian majority in the Balkans to Islam
options.B: give conquered Balkan peoples a share in governing their home provinces
options.C: reward old Turkish noble families with the top posts in the government
options.D: limit the power of noble families and keep central control of the army

rationales.A: Incorrect. The devshirme took selected boys. It was not a plan to convert all the empire's Christians.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Recruits were taken "forever from parents" and served wherever the sultan sent them, not as leaders of their home communities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The system did the reverse. It gave top posts to trained slaves so that noble families would not control them.
rationales.D: Correct. Lybyer says recruits were taken from their parents, had "no certain hold on property," and had "no definite promise" for their children. They could not easily become a rival noble class.

questions.explanation: Rulers in many empires worried about powerful nobles. The Ottoman sultans built a ruling class of men who owed their whole careers to the sultan, which kept power in his hands.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in the late 1500s and 1600s weakened the system Lybyer describes?

options.A: Sultans began choosing grand viziers mainly from old Turkish-born Muslim families.
options.B: Sultans began hiring European mercenaries in place of the Janissaries.
options.C: Janissaries were allowed to marry and enroll their sons in the corps.
options.D: Most Balkan Christians converted, leaving few boys to recruit.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Men of many backgrounds still served as viziers. The bigger change was inside the Janissary corps.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Janissaries stayed at the core of the army until a sultan abolished them in 1826. The change came from inside the corps.
rationales.C: Correct. Lybyer says members were not supposed to have families or pass anything to their children. Once Janissaries married and enrolled their sons, more places went to soldiers' families instead of to trained recruits.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Most Balkan Christians kept their faith. The devshirme faded for other reasons.

questions.explanation: Over the late 1500s and 1600s, many Janissaries married, ran businesses, and enrolled their sons, and other Muslim-born men joined too. The devshirme was used less and less after the mid-1600s. The corps grew larger, less disciplined, and harder for sultans to control.

questions.stem: Shah Isma'il's policy described in the first paragraph is best understood as an effort to

options.A: keep peace in Tabriz by tolerating both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims
options.B: restore the authority of the caliphs over the whole Muslim world
options.C: make Shi'a Islam the state faith and force Sunnis to accept it
options.D: convert the Christian peoples of the Caucasus to Islam by force

rationales.A: Incorrect. Isma'il refused to tolerate Sunnis. He threatened to "leave not one of them alive."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Isma'il ordered the public cursing of the first three caliphs. He did not try to restore their authority.
rationales.C: Correct. Isma'il ordered that Shi'a Islam be "the only tolerated creed" and threatened death to anyone who refused.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The passage is about the Muslims of Tabriz, most of whom were Sunni, not about Christians.

questions.explanation: The Safavids made Shi'a Islam the state religion of Persia. This gave their new dynasty a strong identity and set Persia apart from its Sunni neighbors, the Ottomans and the Uzbeks. Iran remains mostly Shi'a today.

questions.stem: The policies described in the passage contributed most directly to

options.A: long Safavid–Ottoman wars that deepened the split between Sunni and Shi'a
options.B: a Safavid alliance with the Uzbeks against the Ottoman Turks
options.C: an Ottoman–Safavid alliance against the Portuguese traders in the Persian Gulf
options.D: the return of most Persians to Sunni Islam soon after Isma'il's death

rationales.A: Correct. Browne says relations with the Sunni Ottomans were "uniformly hostile." The two empires fought on and off for more than a century, and religion made the rivalry more bitter.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Browne says relations with the Sunni Uzbeks were also "uniformly hostile."
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Ottomans and Safavids were enemies. They did not ally against the Portuguese.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Persia stayed Shi'a after Isma'il died in 1524.

questions.explanation: Ottoman–Safavid wars began with the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 and went on, off and on, until a peace treaty in 1639. Each side called the other an enemy of true Islam, and the fighting hardened the divide between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims.

questions.stem: Selim's letter, described in the third paragraph, was most likely intended to

options.A: invite Isma'il to join the Ottomans in a war against the Habsburgs in Europe
options.B: propose a trade agreement for Persian silk
options.C: offer to accept Isma'il as caliph in exchange for peace
options.D: justify an Ottoman invasion by presenting it as a defense of Sunni Islam

rationales.A: Incorrect. The letter threatens Isma'il. It does not invite him to be an ally.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The letter is about religion and land, not trade.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Selim saw himself as the defender of Sunni Islam and called Isma'il a heretic. He was not offering Isma'il any religious title.
rationales.D: Correct. Selim calls Isma'il's beliefs "heresies," demands that he stop cursing Abu Bakr and 'Umar, and threatens to invade. Religion gave Selim a reason for war.

questions.explanation: Ottoman and Safavid rulers both used religion to rally support. Selim invaded a few months after this letter and defeated Isma'il at Chaldiran in August 1514.

questions.stem: Isma'il's religious policy differed most from that of the Mughal emperor Akbar, who

options.A: required his subjects to follow Sunni law in worship and daily life
options.B: welcomed teachers of many faiths and ended the jizya tax on non-Muslims
options.C: forced his Hindu subjects to convert to Shi'a Islam or leave
options.D: banned Sufi brotherhoods and their shrines from his empire

rationales.A: Incorrect. Akbar did not force Sunni practice on his mostly Hindu subjects.
rationales.B: Correct. Akbar held debates among Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Christians, and others, and he ended the jizya in 1564. Isma'il used force against Sunni Muslims who resisted.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Akbar did not force conversion. Most of his subjects remained Hindu.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Akbar respected Sufis. He walked to the shrine of a Sufi saint at Ajmer.

questions.explanation: Rulers chose different ways to manage religious diversity. Isma'il used force to impose Shi'a Islam on Persia's Sunni Muslims. Akbar, who ruled a mostly Hindu land, chose tolerance to win the loyalty of his diverse subjects.

questions.stem: The data in the table best support which of the following claims?

options.A: Lands taken from the Mamluks in 1516–1517 supplied over half the listed income.
options.B: Anatolia and Greece, the empire's oldest lands, supplied over half the listed income.
options.C: Upper Mesopotamia, taken from the Safavids after 1514, supplied more income than Syria.
options.D: Syria provided more income than Anatolia and Greece.

rationales.A: Correct. Egypt and Syria, which Selim I took from the Mamluks in 1516–1517, together supplied 2,300,000 of the 3,750,000 ducats listed, more than 60 percent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Anatolia and Greece gave 1,300,000 of the 3,750,000 ducats listed, about 35 percent.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Upper Mesopotamia gave 150,000 ducats, much less than Syria's 700,000.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Syria gave 700,000 ducats, about half as much as Anatolia and Greece.

questions.explanation: Egypt alone sent the sultan more than any other region listed. Its Nile farmland and trade made it very valuable. Conquest brought the Ottomans not only land but also large new revenues.

questions.stem: Revenues like those in the table were used mainly to

options.A: pay the sultan's salaried troops, such as the Janissaries, and his court
options.B: pay regular cash salaries to cavalrymen serving under the timar system
options.C: repay loans from Venetian and Genoese bankers
options.D: pay tribute to the Habsburgs to keep peace on the Danube frontier

rationales.A: Correct. The Janissaries and other troops of the sultan's household were paid in cash from the treasury, and the palace and court in Istanbul were costly too.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Timar cavalrymen lived on the taxes from their own assigned lands, not on cash salaries from the treasury.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Ottoman state did not depend on loans from Italian bankers in this period.
rationales.D: Incorrect. It was the reverse. After 1547 the Habsburgs paid the sultan a yearly tribute for their part of Hungary.

questions.explanation: The Janissaries and other household troops were paid in cash, in peace and in war. A steady flow of taxes from rich provinces like Egypt let the sultan keep a large standing army.

questions.stem: Which of the following was an Ottoman method of collecting revenues like those in the table?

options.A: Depending on hereditary zamindars to gather the land revenue
options.B: Selling the right to collect certain taxes to private bidders
options.C: Combining taxes into one silver payment under the "Single Whip"
options.D: Collecting tribute in furs from the forest peoples of the north

rationales.A: Incorrect. Zamindars were local landholders who collected revenue in Mughal India.
rationales.B: Correct. In tax farming, a bidder paid the state for the right to collect a tax and kept whatever he collected beyond that amount. The Ottomans used it widely.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Single Whip reform was a policy of Ming China.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fur tribute was a Russian method in Siberia, not an Ottoman one.

questions.explanation: Empires needed reliable ways to collect taxes. The Ottomans used tax farming, the Mughals used zamindars, and the Ming collected taxes in silver. Each method helped pay for armies and officials.

questions.stem: The Moroccan victory described in the passage is best explained by

options.A: the small size of the Songhai army compared with the invading Moroccan force
options.B: the Songhai army's lack of horsemen to face the Moroccan cavalry
options.C: a revolt by Timbuktu's scholars against the Songhai rulers
options.D: the invaders' firearms and their army organized on the Ottoman model

rationales.A: Incorrect. It was the reverse. Fewer than 4,000 Moroccans defeated 12,000 horsemen and 30,000 foot soldiers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lugard says Songhai sent 12,000 horsemen, more than the whole Moroccan force.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The passage says nothing about a revolt in Timbuktu before the battle.
rationales.D: Correct. The Moroccans were "well armed with muskets," which the Songhai armies lacked, and their army was "reformed on the model of the Turks."

questions.explanation: Like Babur in India, the Moroccan general won with a small army armed with guns. Here, guns and training helped a small force defeat a much larger one, though guns alone did not guarantee victory.

questions.stem: The conflict described in the passage is best understood in the context of

options.A: rivalries over control of trans-Saharan trade in goods such as salt and gold
options.B: European competition for colonies and trading forts in the interior of West Africa
options.C: the spread of the Sunni–Shi'a conflict into West Africa
options.D: the Mali Empire's conquest of Songhai lands

rationales.A: Correct. Morocco's "cause of quarrel" was the Taghaza salt mines, the main salt supply of the region. Morocco's sultan also wanted the gold that came from West Africa.
rationales.B: Incorrect. In the 1500s Europeans traded on the coast. They did not yet compete for colonies inland.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Both Morocco and Songhai were Sunni Muslim states. Their quarrel was over salt and trade.
rationales.D: Incorrect. By the 1500s Mali was weak, and Songhai had taken over much of its land.

questions.explanation: Songhai grew rich from the trade routes that crossed the Sahara, and Morocco's sultan wanted those riches. After the conquest, the Songhai Empire broke apart into smaller states.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the passage as evidence about the Songhai defeat?

options.A: The writer lived 300 years later and saw West Africa through a British imperial lens.
options.B: The writer gives the size of the Moroccan force but not of the Songhai army.
options.C: The writer does not explain why Morocco and Songhai went to war.
options.D: The writer says little about how the Moroccan army was armed and trained.

rationales.A: Correct. Shaw wrote in 1905, while her husband governed Northern Nigeria for Britain. Her phrase "rich and supine populations" and her image of wolves among "flocks of sheep" show a colonial view of Africans as weak.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Shaw gives both: fewer than 4,000 Moroccans against 12,000 horsemen and 30,000 foot soldiers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Shaw names the cause: the quarrel over the salt mines of Tegazza.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Shaw describes the Moroccans' muskets, discipline, and army "reformed on the model of the Turks."

questions.explanation: A limitation is a reason to use a source with care. Shaw's account is useful, but her colonial point of view shaped how she described Africans. She also got the date of the battle wrong. Historians compare her account with the Timbuktu histories themselves.

questions.stem: Bernier's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: the Mughal emperors were too weak to collect taxes from their distant provinces
options.B: peasants in India were better off than peasants in France
options.C: giving grant holders more power over peasants would raise the king's income
options.D: temporary revenue grants led officials to squeeze peasants and harm farming

rationales.A: Incorrect. Bernier says the grant holders had power "almost absolute" over peasants. The problem was harsh collection, not weak collection.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bernier says French peasants had protectors, such as parliaments and judges, while Indian peasants had none.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Bernier argues the opposite. He says the king would gain if private property in land were recognized.
rationales.D: Correct. Bernier says the grant holders "may be deprived of it in a single moment," so they "draw from the soil all the money we can, though the peasant should starve."

questions.explanation: Bernier believed that people work hard only when they can keep what they earn. Because grant holders could lose their grants at any moment, they took all they could. Historians check his claim that the emperor owned all the land against Mughal records.

questions.stem: Which of the following kinds of evidence would most directly challenge Bernier's claim that there was no private property in land in Mughal India?

options.A: Records showing that the emperor assigned provincial tax income to officers
options.B: Records showing that local families inherited and sold rights to land
options.C: Reports that revenue collectors made heavy demands on farmers
options.D: Orders moving officers from one land grant to another after a few years

rationales.A: Incorrect. Assigning tax income to officers fits Bernier's description. It does not show who owned the land.
rationales.B: Correct. Rights to land that families inherited and sold would be private property. Such records would directly challenge Bernier's claim.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Heavy demands show a burden on farmers, which Bernier also describes. They do not show who owned the land.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Frequent transfers show that grants were temporary, which agrees with Bernier.

questions.explanation: Bernier said the king owned all the land. Historians have found records of zamindars and other local families who inherited, bought, and sold rights to land in Mughal India. Such evidence shows that Bernier's claim was too broad.

questions.stem: Mughal emperors used the land grants described in the first paragraph mainly in order to

options.A: turn the empire's nobles into landowners who could pass their grants to their sons
options.B: pay the emperor's officers in cash from a central treasury instead of in land revenue
options.C: keep officers dependent on the emperor by giving them grants that could be taken back
options.D: let peasants buy the land they farmed in return for lower taxes

rationales.A: Incorrect. Most grants were not owned or passed down. Grant holders feared their work would benefit "neither ourselves nor our children."
rationales.B: Incorrect. The grants were given "as an equivalent for their pay," in place of cash salaries.
rationales.C: Correct. Bernier says the grants were given "in lieu of their salary," and holders "may be deprived of it in a single moment." Grants that could be moved or taken away kept officers loyal to the emperor.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bernier says the king was "proprietor of the land" and that private property was not recognized.

questions.explanation: Mughal emperors paid their officers with jagirs, the right to collect the revenue of an area. Most jagirs were moved every few years and were not passed down to sons. This kept nobles from building local power and tied them to the emperor.
